stem:
A 4-month-old girl born at 38 weeks presents to your regional emergency department in July with 3 days of coryza and worsening cough. She is feeding at half her usual volume, has had four wet nappies in 24 hours, and had a brief apnoeic pause at home that resolved with stimulation.

On examination she is alert, mildly tachypnoeic with subcostal recession, and has bilateral fine crackles and wheeze. There is no fever. She has no prior admissions and was well until this illness.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 152, BP 88/54, RR 62, SpO2 89% on room air, temp 37.2 C
data_table.Examination: Alert; capillary refill 2 seconds; peripheries warm; subcostal and intercostal recession; nasal flare absent; bilateral fine crackles with expiratory wheeze
data_table.Investigations: Bedside blood glucose 4.6 mmol/L; NPA pending; chest x-ray not yet performed

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial oxygen therapy?

options.text: Nebulised salbutamol 2.5 mg with 6 litres per minute driving oxygen with cardiac monitoring throughout
High-flow nasal cannula oxygen at 2 litres per kilogram per minute from the outset with cardiac monitoring throughout
Face mask oxygen at 6 litres per minute, titrate to SpO2 at least 94 percent with cardiac monitoring throughout
Continuous positive airway pressure via mask at 5 cm H2O with cardiac monitoring throughout
Nasal prong oxygen at 1 litre per minute, titrate to SpO2 at least 90 percent with cardiac monitoring throughout

stem:
A 2-year-old boy is brought in at 2 am with barking cough and hoarse voice starting after a coryzal illness. His mother says he sounds noisy on breathing in when upset but is quiet when settled on her lap.

On examination he is settled, has a barking cough, and stridor is audible only with agitation. There is mild suprasternal recession when he cries but none at rest. Air entry is symmetrical and there is no wheeze.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 118, BP 96/58, RR 32, SpO2 97 percent on room air, temp 37.6 C
data_table.Examination: Alert, comforted by mother; barking cough; stridor with agitation only; mild suprasternal recession when crying, none at rest

lead_in: What dose of dexamethasone would you give?

options.text: Oral dexamethasone 0.15 mg per kg once now with cardiac monitoring throughout
Oral dexamethasone 0.6 mg per kg once now with cardiac monitoring throughout
Nebulised budesonide 2 mg once now instead of dexamethasone
Oral prednisolone 1 mg per kg once now with cardiac monitoring throughout
Withhold steroid and reassess after 30 minutes of observation

stem:
A 3-year-old girl weighing 15 kg develops a widespread urticarial rash, hoarse voice, and repeated coughing within 5 minutes of eating a peanut biscuit at daycare. Paramedics report she vomited twice on the way to your ED.

On arrival she looks anxious, has audible stridor at rest, and has swollen lips. Circulation is preserved and she is protecting her airway. There is no wheeze on auscultation but transmitted upper airway noise is loud. She has a known peanut allergy on the daycare register.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 148, BP 92/56, RR 34, SpO2 95 percent on room air, temp 36.9 C
data_table.Examination: Widespread urticaria trunk and face; peri-oral and lip swelling; audible stridor at rest; no wheeze; capillary refill 2 seconds

lead_in: What dose of intramuscular adrenaline would you administer first?

options.text: Adrenaline 300 micrograms intramuscularly to the anterolateral thigh
Adrenaline 150 micrograms intramuscularly to the anterolateral thigh
Adrenaline 10 micrograms per kg intramuscularly, calculated to 150 micrograms
Adrenaline 150 micrograms subcutaneously to the anterolateral thigh
Nebulised adrenaline 5 mL of 1:1000 while preparing IM dose

stem:
A 21-day-old boy born at term by uncomplicated vaginal birth is brought to your ED at 3 am. Parents report he has been feeding poorly for 8 hours and had one axillary temperature of 38.3 C at home. He is now afebrile but they describe him as floppy.

On examination he is pale, minimally responsive to nappy change, and has cool peripheries with a capillary refill of 3.5 seconds. Anterior fontanelle is normal. Skin examination shows no rash. Chest is clear and abdomen is soft. There is no organomegaly.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 190, BP 62 systolic, RR 68, SpO2 96 percent on room air, temp 36.1 C
data_table.Examination: Pale, hypotonic, minimally responsive; capillary refill 3.5 s; anterior fontanelle normal; no rash; chest clear; abdomen soft
data_table.Investigations: Bedside glucose 2.4 mmol/L; VBG pH 7.22, lactate 4.8 mmol/L, base excess -9

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management priority?

options.text: Intranasal midazolam for agitation, then oral maintenance rehydration once settled with cardiac monitoring throughout
IV access, blood cultures, empirical IV ceftriaxone with cardiac monitoring with cardiac monitoring throughout
Peripheral IV, blood cultures, and empirical IV amoxicillin with cardiac monitoring with cardiac monitoring throughout
IV access, blood cultures, empirical IV cefotaxime plus benzylpenicillin with cardiac monitoring throughout
Warm and observe with hourly vital signs; hold antibiotics until cultures return with cardiac monitoring

stem:
A 3-year-old girl is referred by her GP after 11 days of fever. Over that time she has developed a rash, red cracked lips, a red tongue, and bilateral non-purulent conjunctivitis. Peeling has started around her fingertips this morning. The parents say the fever came down for the first time yesterday.

On examination she has mild peri-anal desquamation and desquamating fingertips, a single 2 cm cervical lymph node, and a diffuse maculopapular rash on her trunk. Cardiac auscultation is unremarkable and there is no gallop.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 128, BP 96/60, RR 26, SpO2 99 percent on room air, temp 37.4 C
data_table.Investigations: Hb 96 g/L (110-140); WCC 16.4 x10^9/L (4-11); platelets 620 x10^9/L (150-450); CRP 78 mg/L (<5); ALT 74 U/L (<40); albumin 28 g/L (35-50); sodium 132 mmol/L (135-145); urine white cells positive with negative culture
data_table.Echocardiogram: Left main coronary artery Z-score +2.2, right coronary artery Z-score +1.6, no aneurysm; normal LV function

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management now?

options.text: IV methylprednisolone pulse for 3 days and no immunoglobulin with cardiac monitoring throughout
Oral aspirin at antiplatelet dose alone and outpatient echocardiogram follow up in 6 weeks
IV immunoglobulin 2 g per kg over 10 to 12 hours plus oral aspirin at anti-inflammatory dose
Oral ibuprofen for symptom control and reassure that peeling means the illness has run its course
Discharge home on watchful waiting because the fever has settled without treatment

stem:
A 4-year-old girl presents to your rural ED collapsed on the trolley with a history of 24 hours of vomiting and reduced urine output. On arrival she has a purpuric rash on her thighs and cool mottled peripheries.

The nurse has attempted two peripheral IV cannulations in the antecubital fossae unsuccessfully over 4 minutes. She remains poorly perfused with a capillary refill of 5 seconds and is drowsy but rousable.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 168, BP 68 systolic, RR 38, SpO2 96 percent on room air, temp 39.4 C
data_table.Examination: Non-blanching purpuric rash lower limbs and buttocks; capillary refill 5 s; peripheries cool and mottled; GCS 13 (E3 V4 M6)
data_table.Investigations: Bedside glucose 5.8 mmol/L; POC lactate 5.6 mmol/L

lead_in: What is the next best step?

options.text: Central venous line insertion in the right internal jugular vein under ultrasound
Continue attempting peripheral IV access for a further 5 minutes before considering IO
Insert an intraosseous needle in the proximal tibia and draw cultures with cardiac monitoring throughout
IM ceftriaxone 50 mg per kg and continue attempting IV access with cardiac monitoring throughout
Rectal paracetamol 15 mg per kg and re-attempt peripheral IV access when the fever settles

stem:
A 2-year-old boy with known congenital adrenal hyperplasia (21-hydroxylase deficiency) on hydrocortisone and fludrocortisone is brought in with 18 hours of vomiting and lethargy. His parents doubled his oral hydrocortisone at illness onset but he has vomited every dose since. There has been no diarrhoea.

On examination he is drowsy but rousable, has cool peripheries with a capillary refill of 4 seconds, and mucous membranes are dry. Skin turgor is reduced. There is no focal infection on examination and the abdomen is soft with no organomegaly.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 172, BP 74/40, RR 32, SpO2 98 percent on room air, temp 36.8 C
data_table.Examination: Drowsy, capillary refill 4 s; dry mucous membranes; reduced skin turgor; abdomen soft; no rash
data_table.Investigations: Sodium 122 mmol/L (135-145); potassium 6.4 mmol/L (3.5-5.0); glucose 2.6 mmol/L (3.5-6.0); urea 12 mmol/L (2.5-7.5); VBG pH 7.24, HCO3 14 mmol/L, base excess -10; POC lactate 3.2 mmol/L
data_table.Medications: Hydrocortisone 5 mg orally three times daily; fludrocortisone 100 micrograms daily

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Double the oral hydrocortisone dose and admit for observation and repeat as clinically indicated
IV dexamethasone 0.15 mg per kg then oral rehydration when tolerated and repeat as clinically indicated
Calcium gluconate 0.5 mL per kg IV followed by insulin dextrose infusion for hyperkalaemia
3 percent saline 3 mL per kg over 20 minutes for the hyponatraemia and repeat as clinically indicated
IV hydrocortisone 50 mg stat plus 10 percent dextrose 2 mL per kg IV then normal saline 20 mL per kg over 30 minutes

subtopic_detail: Oxygen target in acute paediatric asthma
stem: A 10-year-old girl with a severe asthma exacerbation is receiving back-to-back salbutamol and ipratropium by oxygen-driven nebuliser with oral prednisolone. She is alert and her work of breathing is settling.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 132, RR 28, SpO2 98 percent on 8 L/min, BP 106/66

lead_in: What is the most appropriate oxygen strategy?

options.text: Titrate nasal prong oxygen to oxygen saturations of 92 to 95 percent
Continue 8 L/min by mask to keep oxygen saturations at 100 percent
Titrate nasal prong oxygen to oxygen saturations of 88 to 92 percent
Change to high flow nasal cannula at 2 litres per kilogram each minute
Withhold oxygen entirely and reassess the saturations in one hour

stem:
A 25-day-old term female infant is brought to your regional emergency department by her mother with 6 hours of a rectal temperature of 38.4 C at home. She has been feeding less well since this morning, taking about half her usual volume, and has had two wet nappies today rather than her usual five to six. There has been no cough, coryza, rash or diarrhoea. Delivery was normal vaginal at 39 weeks; the mother's group B streptococcus swab was negative and there was no prolonged rupture of membranes.

On arrival she is lying quietly in her mother's arms with a weak cry when handled and mild peripheral mottling. Anterior fontanelle is soft and flat. There is no rash, no focal source on ear or throat examination, and the chest is clear to auscultation.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 178, BP 72/44, RR 58, SpO2 97% on room air, temp 38.6 C axillary
data_table.Examination: Weak cry; peripheral mottling with capillary refill 3 seconds; anterior fontanelle soft and flat; no rash; ears and throat clear; chest clear; abdomen soft with no organomegaly
data_table.Investigations: Bedside blood glucose 3.9 mmol/L; venous gas pH 7.32 lactate 2.6 mmol/L; urinalysis clean-catch pending

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Take blood cultures and a catheter urine specimen, then observe for 4 hours off antibiotics before deciding on lumbar puncture and empirical therapy
Obtain blood cultures, urine by catheter or suprapubic aspirate, and CSF by lumbar puncture, then give empirical IV benzylpenicillin plus gentamicin without delay
Obtain blood cultures and urine by catheter, start empirical IV benzylpenicillin plus gentamicin, and defer lumbar puncture until the infant is more stable
Obtain blood cultures, urine by catheter, and CSF by lumbar puncture, then give empirical IV ceftriaxone as monotherapy without additional agents
Perform a viral respiratory swab and urinalysis first and give empirical IV benzylpenicillin plus gentamicin only if either result is positive for infection

stem:
A 22-month-old boy weighing 12 kg is brought to your paediatric emergency department with two days of watery diarrhoea, four episodes today of non-bilious vomiting, and reduced oral intake. His parents report he has had three small wet nappies in the last 12 hours and has been less playful than usual but is still recognising them. He has no significant past medical history and immunisations are up to date including rotavirus.

He has been offered oral rehydration solution in the waiting room over the last hour but has vomited each of the three attempts within minutes of drinking. He is tolerating small sips of water in between. There is no blood in the stool and no fever.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 148, BP 92/58, RR 30, SpO2 99% on room air, temp 37.4 C
data_table.Examination: Alert; capillary refill 2 seconds; peripheries warm; mucous membranes dry; skin turgor mildly reduced; no acidotic breathing; abdomen soft and non-tender
data_table.Investigations: Bedside blood glucose 4.8 mmol/L; venous gas pH 7.36 base excess -3 mmol/L; urinalysis specific gravity 1.025

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in rehydration?

options.text: Insert a peripheral intravenous cannula and give a 20 millilitre per kilogram normal saline bolus over 15 minutes
Insert a peripheral intravenous cannula and commence a maintenance rate of 4-2-1 formula plus 5 percent deficit replacement in one third normal saline
Give an oral single dose of ondansetron 4 milligrams and then re-attempt oral rehydration solution by mouth in small aliquots over one hour
Admit for observation with sips of clear fluids only for the next four hours and reassess hydration before making a rehydration plan
Insert a nasogastric tube and commence oral rehydration solution at 25 millilitres per kilogram per hour over the first four hours

stem:
A 2-year-old boy weighing 13 kg presents at 11 pm to your paediatric emergency department with a barking cough that started this evening. He was well earlier in the day with mild coryza for two days. He has a hoarse voice and audible stridor at rest that started 30 minutes ago. His mother reports he settled somewhat in the cool night air on the way in.

On examination he is alert and clinging to his mother. There is intermittent inspiratory stridor at rest with mild sternal recession, no cyanosis, and no drooling. He is speaking in short sentences and has a wet-sounding cough. There is no rash and no fever.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 128, BP 96/60, RR 32, SpO2 96% on room air, temp 37.5 C
data_table.Examination: Alert; peripheries warm; capillary refill 2 seconds; inspiratory stridor at rest with mild sternal recession; no drooling; no cyanosis; chest clear other than transmitted upper airway noise
data_table.Investigations: Not indicated

lead_in: What is the most appropriate steroid regimen?

options.text: Oral dexamethasone 0.15 milligrams per kilogram as a single dose and observe for 3 hours before discharge planning
Oral dexamethasone 0.6 milligrams per kilogram single dose and admit to the paediatric ward for overnight monitoring for 12 hours
Nebulised budesonide 2 milligrams as a single dose delivered over 10 minutes and discharge home after 60 minutes of observation
Oral prednisolone 1 milligram per kilogram single dose and observe for 3 hours before discharge to the community with follow-up
Nebulised adrenaline 5 millilitres of 1:1000 solution first, then oral dexamethasone 0.15 milligrams per kilogram single dose and 3 hour observation

stem:
A 20-month-old girl who had a routine antenatal 20 week morphology scan and follow-up 32 week scan both reporting normal kidneys and urinary tract presents to her general practitioner two weeks after completing a course of oral trimethoprim for a first culture-confirmed E coli urinary tract infection. She had a clean-catch urine sample that grew 100,000 CFU per mL of E coli fully sensitive to trimethoprim. She defervesced within 48 hours of starting antibiotics.

She is otherwise well, meeting developmental milestones, and has no palpable abdominal mass. Her growth trajectory is on the 50th centile and stable. Her mother has heard from a friend that her child should have a renal ultrasound and asks about imaging.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 108, BP 98/60, RR 24, SpO2 100% on room air, temp 36.8 C
data_table.Examination: Alert; no dysmorphism; abdomen soft with no palpable mass; genitalia normal; spine normal with no sacral dimple
data_table.Investigations: Follow-up urine dipstick negative for leucocytes and nitrites; renal function within normal limits from admission bloods

lead_in: What is the most appropriate imaging plan?

options.text: DMSA renal scan at 3 months post infection to exclude renal scarring and vesicoureteric reflux with subsequent decision on prophylactic antibiotics
Renal tract ultrasound within 6 weeks as she is under 24 months of age even though the UTI was typical E coli and antenatal scans were reassuring
No routine imaging required as she has had one typical UTI with documented antenatal renal tract monitoring and rapid response to first line antibiotics
Micturating cystourethrogram at 3 months post infection to exclude vesicoureteric reflux before deciding whether prophylactic antibiotics are indicated
Contrast-enhanced renal MRI at 6 weeks to characterise renal parenchyma with a view to specialist renal outpatient review before repeat culture

stem:
A 6-week-old former term male infant is admitted overnight in July with moderate bronchiolitis. He has been on nasal prong oxygen at 1 litre per minute for the last 2 hours 15 minutes to maintain SpO2 above 90 percent. Immediately before the trial, his SpO2 was 88 percent in room air. Feeds have been paused because he is working too hard to feed.

On the third hourly review he still has moderate subcostal and intercostal recession with fine crackles throughout. His SpO2 is now 90 percent on 1 L per minute nasal prongs but he has had two brief apnoeic episodes in the last hour that resolved with mild stimulation. He is drowsier than at admission but rousable and pink.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 168, BP 76/48, RR 68, SpO2 90% on 1 L/min nasal prong oxygen, temp 37.6 C
data_table.Examination: Drowsy but rousable; moderate subcostal and intercostal recession; nasal flare; capillary refill 2 seconds; peripheries warm; bilateral fine crackles with wheeze; two brief apnoeic episodes in the last hour resolving with stimulation
data_table.Investigations: Venous gas pH 7.30 pCO2 55 mmHg bicarbonate 27 mmol/L base excess 0 mmol/L; NPA positive for RSV; chest x-ray hyperinflation without focal consolidation

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in respiratory support?

options.text: Continue low-flow nasal prong oxygen at 2 litres per minute and reassess in another 2 hours with continuous cardiorespiratory monitoring in place
Give hypertonic saline 3 percent nebulised 4 millilitres and continue current low-flow nasal prong oxygen at 1 litre per minute with 2 hourly review
Trial nebulised salbutamol 0.5 milligrams via 6 litres per minute driving oxygen every 20 minutes for 3 doses and reassess work of breathing
Commence bubble continuous positive airway pressure at 5 centimetres of water via mask and defer PICU discussion until this fails
Escalate to high-flow nasal cannula oxygen at 2 litres per kilogram per minute with FiO2 titrated to SpO2 90 percent and PICU liaison for potential transfer

subtopic_detail: Anaphylaxis adrenaline dose, route and concentration
stem:
A 4-year-old boy weighing 18 kg is brought to a metropolitan emergency department 10 minutes after eating a cashew biscuit at a birthday party. He has a known peanut allergy but has not reacted to tree nuts before. Hives appeared within 5 minutes, followed by a hoarse voice and noisy breathing.

He has no adrenaline autoinjector with him and IV access has not yet been obtained. Adrenaline 1 mg/mL (1:1000) and 0.1 mg/mL (1:10 000) ampoules are on the resuscitation trolley.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 148 /min, blood pressure 78/44 mmHg, respiratory rate 40 /min, SpO2 93% on room air, temperature 36.7°C
data_table.Examination: Anxious, speaking in short phrases; generalised urticaria; lip and periorbital swelling; biphasic stridor; audible expiratory wheeze; capillary refill 3 seconds with cool peripheries

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first dose of adrenaline?

options.text: IM adrenaline 1 mg/mL, 0.1 mg/kg (1.8 mL), into the anterolateral thigh
SC adrenaline 1 mg/mL, 0.01 mg/kg (0.18 mL), into the deltoid of the upper arm
IM adrenaline 1 mg/mL, 0.01 mg/kg (0.18 mL), into the anterolateral thigh
IV adrenaline 0.1 mg/mL, 0.01 mg/kg (1.8 mL), as a bolus once IV access is gained
Nebulised adrenaline 1 mg/mL, 5 mL, by mask, deferring IM until the stridor settles

stem:
A 3-year-old girl weighing 14 kg presents to a regional emergency department with 24 hours of fever to 40 C, poor feeding, and vomiting. She has been progressively drowsy since arrival. IV access was obtained on the second attempt, blood cultures drawn, and IV ceftriaxone 100 mg/kg given within 30 minutes of arrival. She then received a 20 mL/kg normal saline bolus over 10 minutes.

Twenty minutes after completion of the first bolus she remains drowsy with cool peripheries and a mottled trunk. Her mucous membranes are dry and she has no purpuric rash. Her lactate has fallen from 5.2 to 4.4 mmol/L but her mean arterial pressure remains at 45 mmHg with a capillary refill of 4 seconds.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 168, BP 78/52 (MAP 45), RR 34, SpO2 96% on 6 L/min via Hudson mask, temp 39.6 C
data_table.Examination: Drowsy but rousable; cool mottled peripheries; capillary refill 4 seconds; no purpuric rash; abdomen soft; chest clear
data_table.Investigations: Venous gas pH 7.24 lactate 4.4 mmol/L base excess -8 mmol/L; sodium 138 potassium 4.2 creatinine 62 mmol/L; INR 1.1

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Repeat 20 millilitre per kilogram normal saline bolus over 10 minutes then reassess perfusion and lactate before considering inotropes
Commence peripheral adrenaline infusion at 0.05 micrograms per kilogram per minute now and defer further crystalloid until inotropes are running
Give a 20 millilitre per kilogram albumin 4 percent bolus over 15 minutes now rather than a second crystalloid bolus to expand intravascular volume
Give intravenous hydrocortisone 2 milligrams per kilogram now for possible adrenal insufficiency before proceeding with any further fluid resuscitation
Intubate for airway protection with cuffed tube and ketamine plus rocuronium induction before further fluid resuscitation is undertaken

subtopic_detail: Paediatric DKA fluid management in shock
stem:
A 10-year-old girl weighing 30 kg presents to your paediatric emergency department with 2 days of polyuria, polydipsia, and progressive drowsiness. There is no known past history of diabetes. She was found by her father this morning slumped in bed and rousable only to voice.

On arrival she is drowsy with deep sighing respiration and a fruity odour on her breath. Peripheries are cool with capillary refill of 4 seconds and mucous membranes are dry. Her airway is patent and she is protecting it. She has no focal neurology and no signs of raised intracranial pressure. She is now on the ED trolley with IV access secured.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 138, BP 88/54 (MAP 65), RR 32 deep, SpO2 98% on room air, temp 36.9 C
data_table.Examination: Drowsy but rousable (GCS 12); Kussmaul breathing; cool peripheries with capillary refill 4 seconds; dry mucous membranes; abdomen soft; no focal neurology; pupils equal and reactive
data_table.Investigations: Bedside blood glucose 32 mmol/L; venous gas pH 7.05 bicarbonate 6 mmol/L base excess -22; ketones 5.6 mmol/L; sodium 128 potassium 5.4 chloride 96 corrected sodium 132; urinalysis ketones 4+ glucose 4+

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial fluid regimen?

options.text: Give a 20 millilitre per kilogram normal saline bolus over 15 minutes then commence maintenance plus deficit calculated over 48 hours with an insulin infusion at 0.05 units per kilogram per hour after 1 hour of fluid
Insert nasogastric tube for gastric decompression then commence isotonic saline maintenance without a bolus and start subcutaneous rapid-acting insulin analogue every 4 hours
Start intravenous sodium bicarbonate 1 milliequivalent per kilogram over 1 hour and commence insulin infusion immediately at 0.1 units per kilogram per hour to reverse the ketoacidosis

Give a 20 millilitre per kilogram Hartmann's solution bolus over 15 minutes then commence Plasma-Lyte 148 maintenance plus deficit over 24 hours with insulin infusion at 0.1 units per kilogram per hour from the outset
Give a 10 millilitre per kilogram normal saline bolus over 30 to 60 minutes then commence maintenance plus deficit over 48 hours with insulin infusion at 0.05 to 0.1 units per kilogram per hour

subtopic_detail: Incomplete Kawasaki diagnosis and treatment window
stem:
A 5-month-old male infant presents to your regional paediatric ward on day 8 of fever to 39 C. He has had irritability, a fine erythematous rash on the trunk that came and went, and mild coryza. Empirical amoxicillin was started at day 3 by his general practitioner without effect. He was seen at day 5 in your ED and a septic screen including blood cultures was negative, and he was discharged home with reassurance.

He has been reviewed today by the paediatric registrar. He now has bilateral non-purulent conjunctival injection, redness of the lips with cracking, and mild peripheral extremity swelling. There is no cervical lymphadenopathy. His mother reports his fingertips have started peeling this morning. He continues to have daily fevers.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 158, BP 88/52, RR 40, SpO2 98% on room air, temp 39.1 C
data_table.Examination: Alert but irritable; bilateral bulbar conjunctival injection without exudate; erythematous cracked lips without ulceration; mild non-pitting oedema of the hands; fine peeling of fingertips; no cervical lymphadenopathy; no gallop or murmur; capillary refill 2 seconds
data_table.Investigations: White cell count 18 x10^9/L; platelets 620 x10^9/L; C-reactive protein 145 mg/L; ESR 78 mm/hr; alanine transaminase 92 U/L; albumin 28 g/L; urinalysis 30 white cells per high power field with no organisms; echocardiogram shows a right coronary artery Z score of 2.6

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next management step?

options.text: Give intravenous immunoglobulin 2 grams per kilogram over 10 to 12 hours plus oral aspirin 3 to 5 milligrams per kilogram per day and arrange formal cardiology review
Await repeat inflammatory markers in 48 hours before treating with intravenous immunoglobulin as he does not meet the 4 of 5 principal criteria for complete Kawasaki disease
Give intravenous methylprednisolone 30 milligrams per kilogram daily for 3 days as first-line treatment while withholding intravenous immunoglobulin because of infection risk
Start intravenous ceftriaxone 50 milligrams per kilogram daily and vancomycin pending repeat blood cultures given persistent fever and irritability
Prescribe oral aspirin 30 milligrams per kilogram per day monotherapy and reassess with echocardiogram in 6 weeks before deciding on intravenous immunoglobulin

stem:
A 12-day-old female infant delivered at 36 weeks by uncomplicated caesarean is admitted to your regional special care nursery with 8 hours of poor feeding, lethargy, and one episode of a brief focal right-sided upper limb clonic movement lasting 30 seconds. She had been feeding well at home since discharge on day 4. The mother was group B streptococcus positive and received one dose of intrapartum benzylpenicillin 4 hours before delivery.

On arrival the infant is lethargic with a bulging anterior fontanelle and increased tone. Her cardiovascular examination is unremarkable with capillary refill 2 seconds and warm peripheries. Blood cultures and CSF have been drawn. Head ultrasound at the bedside shows echogenicity in the periventricular white matter but no hydrocephalus or established parenchymal lesion.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 152, BP 68/40, RR 42, SpO2 98% on room air, temp 38.4 C axillary
data_table.Examination: Lethargic; anterior fontanelle bulging; tone increased in all four limbs; no rash; abdomen soft with liver 2 cm below costal margin; peripheries warm; brief focal right upper limb clonic movement witnessed
data_table.Investigations: White cell count 24 x10^9/L neutrophils 15; CRP 88 mg/L; venous gas pH 7.34 lactate 3.1 mmol/L; blood glucose 3.8 mmol/L; CSF opening pressure not measured, WBC 480 per microlitre (85 percent polymorphs), protein 2.1 g/L, glucose 1.4 mmol/L (paired serum 4.8), Gram stain pending

lead_in: What is the most appropriate empirical antimicrobial regimen?

options.text: Intravenous benzylpenicillin plus gentamicin at the standard neonatal doses without additional agents pending culture results
Intravenous cefotaxime at meningitic dosing plus benzylpenicillin plus aciclovir intravenous at 20 milligrams per kilogram three times daily
Intravenous ceftriaxone at 100 milligrams per kilogram daily plus vancomycin at 15 milligrams per kilogram every 6 hours as the primary empirical regimen
Intravenous flucloxacillin plus gentamicin plus a single dose of intravenous dexamethasone 0.15 milligrams per kilogram before the first antibiotic dose
Intravenous meropenem 40 milligrams per kilogram every 8 hours as monotherapy empirically pending sensitivity results and cerebrospinal fluid PCR

stem: A 4-month-old term male infant presents to your rural emergency department in July with 3 days of coryza and 24 hours of worsening cough and feed refusal. He weighs 6 kg and is on nasal prong oxygen 1 L/min. Bedside nasopharyngeal aspirate is positive for RSV. There is no history of prematurity, congenital heart disease or immune compromise.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 168, RR 68, SpO2 89 percent on 1 L/min NP, temp 37.9 C
data_table.Examination: Head bobbing, moderate subcostal and intercostal recessions, widespread wheeze and fine crackles, capillary refill 2 seconds
data_table.Investigations: Bedside gas pH 7.34, pCO2 48 mmHg, lactate 1.4 mmol/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in oxygen delivery?

options.text: Commence heated humidified high flow nasal cannula at 2 L/kg/min via age-appropriate interface, titrating FiO2 to keep SpO2 92 to 96 percent
Continue nasal prong oxygen at 1 L/min and add regular nebulised salbutamol 2.5 mg every 20 minutes with careful cardiorespiratory monitoring
Change to non-rebreather mask at 15 L/min and give nebulised adrenaline 5 mg with oral dexamethasone 0.6 mg/kg for prompt symptomatic relief
Continue nasal prong oxygen at 1 L/min and administer a 20 mL/kg normal saline bolus intravenously over 15 minutes to improve tissue perfusion
Intubate and ventilate at pressure control 22/6 with FiO2 60 percent and admit to the local high dependency bed for ongoing ventilatory management

stem: A 3-year-old Aboriginal boy presents to your remote community clinic with 24 hours of right ear pain, fever to 38.5 C and irritability. He has had two prior otitis media episodes this year. On otoscopy the right tympanic membrane is bulging, red and opaque without perforation. He is systemically well, feeding, alert and drinking normally with no mastoid tenderness and no facial nerve involvement.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 118, RR 24, SpO2 99 percent, temp 38.5 C
data_table.Examination: Right TM bulging, red, opaque; no perforation, no discharge; contralateral TM normal; no mastoid swelling; hydration adequate

lead_in: What is the most appropriate antibiotic decision?

options.text: Symptomatic treatment with paracetamol only and review in 48 hours to reassess before starting any antibiotic therapy for the ear infection
Oral amoxicillin 30 mg/kg twice daily for 7 days plus regular paracetamol for symptom relief, with safety-net review in 48 hours if not improving
Oral amoxicillin 15 mg/kg three times daily for 5 days plus regular paracetamol for symptomatic relief throughout the treatment course
Oral amoxicillin-clavulanate 22.5 mg/kg twice daily for 7 days as first line to cover beta-lactamase producing pathogens implicated in recurrent disease
Intramuscular ceftriaxone 50 mg/kg as a single dose plus oral paracetamol and clinical review in the community clinic the following day

stem: A 5-year-old girl presents to your general practice with 6 months of hard infrequent bowel motions, faecal soiling of her underwear four times a week, and abdominal pain. On abdominal examination there is a firm indentable mass in the left iliac fossa reaching to the umbilicus. There is no vomiting, growth is on the 50th centile, and there is no history of delayed passage of meconium.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 92, RR 18, temp 36.7 C, weight 18 kg
data_table.Examination: Alert well-hydrated child; abdomen soft with palpable faecal mass in left iliac fossa; perianal skin intact; no anal fissure seen on inspection

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first step in management?

options.text: Refer to paediatric surgery for a manual disimpaction under general anaesthesia within the next two weeks in her local paediatric surgical service
Prescribe daily microlax rectal enemas for 3 days plus a fibre-rich diet and increased fluids while awaiting response before further review
Escalating oral macrogol regimen starting at 4 sachets on day 1 and increasing by 2 sachets daily for up to 7 days until liquid stool is passed
Prescribe daily lactulose 10 mL twice daily and review her again in 4 weeks to reassess symptoms, stool pattern and any need for further therapy
Arrange abdominal x-ray and rectal biopsy to exclude Hirschsprung disease and other structural causes before starting any pharmacological therapy for constipation

stem: A 6-year-old boy weighing 22 kg presents to your emergency department 20 minutes after eating a peanut biscuit. He has facial swelling, an urticarial rash on his chest, hoarse voice and stridor at rest. His mother has an EpiPen Jr (150 microgram) at home but did not use it. He has no cardiovascular collapse, IV access has just been secured, and he has no history of asthma.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 148, BP 92/60, RR 34, SpO2 94 percent room air, temp 36.9 C
data_table.Examination: Facial and lip swelling, hoarse voice, stridor at rest, widespread urticaria; chest with mild wheeze; capillary refill 2 seconds

lead_in: What is the immediate adrenaline dose and route you would give?

options.text: Adrenaline 150 microgram intramuscular into the mid-anterolateral thigh, repeated every 5 minutes if no response and rising respiratory distress
Adrenaline 300 microgram intravenous bolus given over 60 seconds, then commence a maintenance intravenous infusion at 0.1 microgram/kg/min for sustained cover
Adrenaline 500 microgram intramuscular into the deltoid muscle, repeated every 5 minutes if no adequate response to the initial dose is observed
Adrenaline 220 microgram intramuscular into the mid-anterolateral thigh (0.22 mL of 1:1000), repeated every 5 minutes as needed if no clinical response
Adrenaline 220 microgram nebulised via 6 L/min oxygen mask, plus IV hydrocortisone 100 mg for airway swelling and cardiovascular protection during transport

stem: A previously well 4-year-old girl presents to your paediatric emergency department with a 3 day history of new petechiae and bruising, appearing after a viral illness 2 weeks earlier. She has no active mucosal bleeding, no melaena and no headache. Examination shows scattered petechiae on trunk and limbs, some shin ecchymoses, and no hepatosplenomegaly or lymphadenopathy. She feels well and is playing normally in the cubicle.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 96, RR 22, BP 100/62, SpO2 99 percent, temp 37.1 C
data_table.Examination: Petechiae trunk and limbs, wet purpura absent, no oral bleeding, no hepatosplenomegaly, no lymphadenopathy
data_table.Investigations: Hb 122, WCC 7.1, platelets 9 x 10^9/L, film shows large platelets and no blasts; coagulation studies normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Admit for a 5 day course of oral prednisolone 2 mg/kg daily and repeat the platelet count on day 5 before deciding on inpatient discharge
Admit for a single dose of IV immunoglobulin 0.8 g/kg over 6 hours and repeat platelet count at 24 hours to assess treatment response and safety
Admit for a single dose of anti-D immunoglobulin 50 microgram/kg intravenously as first-line therapy to raise the platelet count promptly overnight
Perform urgent bone marrow aspirate and trephine to exclude acute leukaemia before starting any specific therapy for the thrombocytopenia observed today
Discharge home on active observation with strict return precautions and follow up review in the outpatient paediatric clinic one week from today

stem: A 12-year-old girl with new onset type 1 diabetes has completed 20 hours of DKA management on your paediatric high dependency unit. She weighs 44 kg and is on an IV insulin infusion at 0.05 units/kg/hour with maintenance fluids and dextrose. She is fully alert, tolerating oral fluids, hungry, and has passed urine three times. Venous gas pH 7.34, bicarbonate 18 mmol/L, beta-hydroxybutyrate 0.4 mmol/L, glucose 9.2 mmol/L.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 92, BP 118/70, RR 16, SpO2 99 percent, temp 36.8 C
data_table.Examination: Fully alert, well hydrated, no abdominal tenderness, no Kussmaul breathing, no focal neurology
data_table.Investigations: Venous pH 7.34, bicarbonate 18 mmol/L, glucose 9.2 mmol/L, ketones 0.4 mmol/L, sodium 138, potassium 4.1

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in insulin management?

options.text: Give subcutaneous long-acting insulin glargine 0.3 units/kg now, continue the IV insulin infusion for 2 hours, then stop the infusion at breakfast time
Cease the IV insulin infusion now and commence oral carbohydrate with correction doses of rapid-acting insulin only given when the meals are actually eaten
Increase the IV insulin infusion to 0.1 units/kg/hour and continue at this higher rate for another 6 hours before attempting subcutaneous transition to insulin
Give a single subcutaneous dose of rapid-acting insulin lispro 0.15 units/kg, cease IV infusion 15 minutes later and place her nil by mouth for observation
Continue the IV insulin infusion overnight and reassess for subcutaneous transition when the endocrine consultant reviews her in the morning ward round

subtopic_detail: Nephrotic syndrome first relapse steroid regimen
stem: A 6-year-old boy with steroid-sensitive nephrotic syndrome, in remission for 4 months after his initial 12 week prednisolone course, presents to your general paediatric clinic with 3 days of periorbital swelling and morning-tested urinary protein 3 plus on dipstick at home. He is well with normal blood pressure and passing urine normally. Weight is 24 kg. There is no history of thromboembolism or infection.

data_table.Examination: Periorbital and mild pretibial oedema, no ascites, no scrotal oedema, chest clear
data_table.Investigations: Urine dipstick protein 3+; serum albumin 22 g/L; creatinine 40 micromol/L (baseline 40)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate steroid regimen for this first relapse?

options.text: Oral prednisolone 60 mg/m2 daily for 6 weeks, then 40 mg/m2 alternate days for 6 weeks and taper over a further 8 weeks over subsequent visits
Oral prednisolone 60 mg/m2 daily until urine is protein-free for 3 consecutive days, then 40 mg/m2 on alternate days for 4 weeks and then stop
Oral cyclophosphamide 2 mg/kg daily for 12 weeks with pneumocystis prophylaxis, as prednisolone should be avoided in this first-relapse presentation for now
Intravenous methylprednisolone 500 mg/m2 daily for 3 days, then oral prednisolone 60 mg/m2 daily for 4 weeks and review the case for renal biopsy referral
Oral tacrolimus 0.1 mg/kg twice daily aiming for a trough level of 4 to 8 microgram/L and cease prednisolone entirely to avoid growth impact for now

stem: A 3-day-old term male infant is brought to your regional emergency department after collapsing at home during a feed. He is grey, mottled and floppy. Femoral pulses are absent and brachial pulses weak. Urgent echocardiogram by the paediatric cardiology fellow shows critical coarctation with a restrictive ductus arteriosus. You commence PGE1 at 0.05 microgram/kg/min. Over 30 minutes SpO2 rises to 88 percent but he becomes progressively apnoeic, hypotonic and temperature drops to 35.4 C. Weight 3.2 kg.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 172, BP 54/28 (right arm), SpO2 pre-ductal 82 to 88 percent, post-ductal 76 percent, temp 35.4 C, RR now 6
data_table.Examination: Grey infant, apnoeic episodes 20 seconds, capillary refill 4 seconds, femoral pulses now palpable, brachial pulses stronger
data_table.Investigations: Venous pH 7.18, lactate 6.8 mmol/L, glucose 3.4 mmol/L, potassium 4.9 mmol/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in his airway and infusion management?

options.text: Reduce the PGE1 infusion to 0.01 microgram/kg/min and continue high flow nasal cannula oxygen at 2 L/kg/min for further ventilatory support and stabilisation
Give caffeine citrate 20 mg/kg IV as loading dose, continue nasal prong oxygen and continue PGE1 at 0.05 microgram/kg/min for the retrieval transfer
Intubate and ventilate now, continue PGE1 at 0.05 microgram/kg/min, then titrate the infusion down to the lowest effective dose of 0.01 to 0.02 microgram/kg/min
Cease PGE1 infusion, give a 20 mL/kg normal saline fluid bolus and administer IV adrenaline 10 microgram/kg for the cardiovascular shock and hypoperfusion
Increase PGE1 to 0.1 microgram/kg/min for maximal ductal patency, apply CPAP 5 cm H2O and rewarm the infant using a radiant warmer during preparation for transfer

stem: A term 40+1 week newborn is delivered at your regional level 2 nursery after a shoulder dystocia and 8 minute delay to first breath. Cord arterial pH is 6.92 with base excess -18 mmol/L. At 30 minutes of age he is intubated and ventilated with adequate saturations. On assessment at 60 minutes of age he has a weak grasp reflex, absent suck, hypotonia in all four limbs and a single brief self-terminating clonic seizure. He weighs 3400 g and is on minimal ventilator settings.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 128, RR ventilated, SpO2 96 percent, temp 37.1 C
data_table.Examination: Weak grasp, absent suck, generalised hypotonia; one 20 second right arm clonic seizure at 55 minutes; anterior fontanelle soft; pupils reactive
data_table.Investigations: Cord arterial pH 6.92 (>=7.00), base excess -18 mmol/L (>=-12), lactate 12 mmol/L (<2), Apgar 2/5/6, blood glucose 3.2 mmol/L (2.6 to 5.5)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in his management?

options.text: Maintain normothermia at 36.8 to 37.2 C, load with phenobarbital 20 mg/kg intravenously and arrange non-urgent transfer to the tertiary nursery for further evaluation
Actively warm to 37.5 C, load with phenytoin 20 mg/kg intravenously and observe locally as one brief self-terminating seizure does not meet criteria for active intervention beyond warmth
Begin passive cooling by turning off the overhead radiant warmer, aim for core temperature 33.5 C and arrange urgent NETS retrieval to a tertiary NICU for active whole-body cooling
Continue mechanical ventilation only, defer any temperature or antiseizure decision until formal amplitude-integrated EEG is available in 2 hours, then reassess encephalopathy grade
Give a 20 mL/kg normal saline bolus intravenously then 10 percent dextrose infusion at 4 mL/kg/hour, hold on cooling until circulatory status is optimised over the next 4 to 6 hours

stem: An 8-year-old boy attends your general practice with his mother because he still wets the bed most nights. He has never had a period longer than 2 dry weeks. He passes urine normally by day, has no daytime wetting, no urgency and no straining. Bowel habit is soft daily motions. He is otherwise well, thriving on the 60th centile and doing well at school socially and academically. His father wet the bed until age 10. Urinalysis is normal.

data_table.Vital signs: Within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Abdomen soft, no palpable bladder, no lower limb neurology, normal external genitalia; spine unremarkable
data_table.Investigations: Urinalysis negative for glucose, protein, leukocytes and nitrites; MSU not required

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first-line management step to offer?

options.text: Desmopressin melt 120 microgram sublingually 30 minutes before bed for a 3 month trial with fluid restriction from the evening meal until morning
Oxybutynin 2.5 mg orally twice daily plus a fluid diary and reassess in 3 months with a bladder ultrasound if no improvement in wetting frequency by then
Refer for urodynamic studies and renal tract ultrasound to exclude an underlying structural or neurological cause before starting any behavioural or pharmacological therapy
Star chart and reward-based lifting overnight at midnight for 6 weeks with no other therapy, reviewing progress at the next school health check appointment
Enuresis alarm program (bell and pad) for a minimum of 8 to 12 weeks with weekly review and continuation until 14 consecutive dry nights are achieved

stem: A 13-year-old boy weighing 84 kg presents to your emergency department with a 3-week history of intermittent right knee pain and a limp that has worsened over the past 48 hours. There is no history of trauma. On examination he keeps the right leg externally rotated at rest and has pain on internal rotation of the right hip. Passive hip flexion produces obligatory external rotation. He is otherwise systemically well.

data_table.Vital signs: Within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Right leg held externally rotated; pain on internal rotation of right hip; obligatory external rotation on hip flexion; no effusion at the knee; distal neurovascular status intact
data_table.Investigations: BMI 32 kg/m2 (5th to 85th centile); no fever, no elevated CRP

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Prescribe ibuprofen 10 mg/kg orally three times daily for 5 days, gentle range of motion physiotherapy and outpatient orthopaedic review in 2 weeks if symptoms persist
Order urgent AP and frog-lateral pelvic X-rays, immediate strict non-weight bearing on crutches and refer urgently to the on-call orthopaedic team for probable in situ pinning
Order an MRI of the knee and both hips within 48 hours with orthopaedic outpatient review to plan definitive management after imaging is available
Arrange bone scan and refer to endocrinology for hypothyroidism and growth hormone screening as a metabolic underlying cause before orthopaedic intervention is planned
Discharge home with paracetamol 500 mg orally four times daily, reassurance about likely Osgood-Schlatter disease and a physiotherapy referral for quadriceps strengthening review

stem: A 9-month-old previously well boy presents to your emergency department with his mother, who reports 6 hours of episodes where he suddenly starts crying, draws both legs up to his chest, then settles quietly for 15 to 20 minutes before crying out again. He has vomited twice, most recently a small amount that looked greenish. His last nappy 30 minutes ago contained slimy red jelly-like material. He is now floppy between the episodes and hard to wake for feeds.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 168, RR 40, SpO2 97 percent on room air, temp 37.4 C, cap refill 3 seconds
data_table.Examination: Between episodes: pale, hypotonic, drowsy but rousable; abdomen soft with a firm sausage-shaped mass palpable in the right upper quadrant; empty right iliac fossa; nappy contents as described
data_table.Investigations: VBG pH 7.32, lactate 3.2 mmol/L (<2)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next diagnostic step?

options.text: Abdominal X-ray series (supine and erect) to identify a target sign, dilated loops or free air before proceeding to more advanced imaging or surgical consultation
Computed tomography of the abdomen and pelvis with intravenous contrast to identify a lead point and any associated bowel ischaemia before contacting the surgical team
Trial of intramuscular ondansetron 0.15 mg/kg with 4 hours of clinical observation and repeat clinical examination before ordering any radiological investigations
Urgent abdominal ultrasound performed by an experienced operator to look for a target sign and to guide the paediatric surgical team's decision on air enema reduction
Take directly to theatre for laparotomy and manual reduction on clinical grounds without waiting for imaging as the classical clinical triad alone is diagnostic and time is critical here

stem: A term 5-week-old formula-fed infant is brought to your GP clinic by her mother because she still looks yellow. Birth weight was 3.4 kg and she now weighs 4.6 kg with normal weight gain. Her mother reports that her nappies contain pale-white stools and her wee looks dark like apple juice over the past week. She is otherwise feeding well, alert and interactive between feeds. She was born vaginally without complication and has no family history of liver disease.

data_table.Vital signs: Within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Jaundice extending below the umbilicus; sclera icteric; abdomen soft with liver edge palpable 3 cm below costal margin, firm; spleen not palpable; no dysmorphism
data_table.Investigations: Total bilirubin 165 micromol/L, conjugated bilirubin 62 micromol/L (<20 micromol/L or <20 percent of total), ALT 145 U/L (<40), GGT 340 U/L (<50); FBC and film normal, blood group compatible, TFTs normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Urgent same-day referral to the paediatric hepatology unit for confirmation of biliary atresia by HIDA scan and liver biopsy with a view to Kasai portoenterostomy
Reassure the mother that this is likely breast milk jaundice or delayed physiological jaundice and review in 4 weeks with a repeat serum bilirubin at that visit
Commence phototherapy at home and repeat serum bilirubin in 48 hours to check the trend before deciding on further evaluation or hospital-based investigations for the persistent jaundice
Start ursodeoxycholic acid 20 mg/kg/day orally and arrange outpatient hepatology review in 4 to 6 weeks with repeat liver function testing before that appointment
Order TORCH serology and metabolic screening (urine reducing substances, plasma amino acids, galactose-1-phosphate) and review results before deciding on any referral pathway

stem: A term 3.6 kg male newborn on your postnatal ward has not passed meconium 52 hours after birth. He has started vomiting greenish material with the last two feeds. His abdomen is distended and tympanic. Rectal examination causes a gush of gas and loose meconium. He was born vaginally at 39+5 weeks after an uncomplicated pregnancy. His mother had gestational diabetes controlled on diet and there is no family history of cystic fibrosis or gastrointestinal disease.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 158, RR 52, SpO2 97 percent, temp 36.9 C
data_table.Examination: Marked abdominal distension, tympanic to percussion; audible bowel sounds; per rectum: normal anus, high tone; gush of gas and loose meconium after examination; no anal pit or fistula
data_table.Investigations: Antenatal screening normal; newborn screen taken day 2, results pending; abdominal X-ray shows dilated bowel loops with paucity of gas in the rectum

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next investigation?

options.text: Sweat chloride testing on day of life 14 to exclude cystic fibrosis after ensuring adequate weight gain and hydration prior to arranging the definitive test
Trial of a warm normal saline enema 10 mL/kg with observation for spontaneous passage of meconium then reassess feeding tolerance over the next 24 to 48 hours
Contrast enema with water-soluble contrast to identify a transition zone and refer to the paediatric surgical team for suction rectal biopsy to confirm Hirschsprung disease
Upper gastrointestinal contrast series to evaluate for malrotation and volvulus given the bilious vomiting before considering lower gastrointestinal contrast studies or rectal biopsies
Anorectal manometry to test the rectosphincteric inhibitory reflex within 24 hours before proceeding to any imaging or surgical review as this is more specific for aganglionosis

stem: A previously well 12-day-old term male infant is brought to your regional emergency department floppy and grey after 2 days of poor feeding and vomiting. Birth weight was 3.5 kg; today he is 3.0 kg. He has been passing normal urine. Newborn screening samples were taken on day 3 and results are not yet back. On examination he is peripherally cool with prolonged capillary refill at 4 seconds and looks profoundly unwell. He has hyperpigmentation of the scrotum and penile shaft is prominent for age. There is no family history of endocrine disease.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 190, RR 62, SpO2 96 percent, temp 36.4 C, cap refill 4 seconds
data_table.Examination: Ashen and mottled; sunken fontanelle; dry mucous membranes; hyperpigmented scrotum; virilised external genitalia; abdomen soft with liver edge 2 cm below costal margin; no rash
data_table.Investigations: Na 118 mmol/L (135 to 145), K 7.2 mmol/L (3.5 to 5.5), glucose 2.1 mmol/L (2.6 to 5.5), urea 12 mmol/L (2.5 to 7.0), creatinine 96 micromol/L (<40), VBG pH 7.19, HCO3 12 mmol/L (22 to 26), lactate 4.5 mmol/L (<2)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: IV bolus 20 mL/kg Hartmann solution over 15 minutes and empirical IV ceftriaxone 50 mg/kg to cover late-onset sepsis while awaiting blood culture and lumbar puncture results
IV dextrose 10 percent bolus 2 mL/kg to correct hypoglycaemia and IV furosemide 1 mg/kg to force diuresis for the hyperkalaemia while further electrolyte studies are sent to laboratory
IV bolus 20 mL/kg normal saline over 15 minutes and IV dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg stat as it provides pure glucocorticoid activity without confounding future stimulation test results
IV bolus 10 mL/kg 5 percent human albumin over 30 minutes and start IV insulin actrapid 0.1 unit/kg/hour with continuous cardiac monitoring for the hyperkalaemia
IV bolus 20 mL/kg normal saline with 5 percent dextrose over 15 minutes, IV hydrocortisone 25 mg stat, IV calcium gluconate 0.5 mL/kg 10 percent for cardioprotection and urgent NETS retrieval

subtopic_detail: Cyanotic newborn - TGA vs pulmonary atresia
stem: A 6-hour-old term newborn on your rural nursery has central cyanosis noted on first feed. He was born vaginally after uncomplicated pregnancy weighing 3.5 kg. He has no respiratory distress and feeds well when calm. Antenatal ultrasound was performed at 20 weeks locally and did not identify a cardiac abnormality. A hyperoxia test with FiO2 1.0 for 10 minutes shows pre-ductal SpO2 rising only from 76 percent to 82 percent. Chest X-ray shows a narrow mediastinum with an egg-on-side cardiac silhouette. Femoral pulses are equal and easily palpable.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 148, RR 46, SpO2 76 percent room air pre-ductal, SpO2 82 percent post-hyperoxia, temp 36.7 C
data_table.Examination: Central cyanosis, mild tachypnoea, no recessions; single loud second heart sound; no murmur; femoral pulses equal; liver at costal margin
data_table.Investigations: Chest X-ray: narrow superior mediastinum, egg-on-side cardiac silhouette, oligaemic lung fields; hyperoxia test as above; VBG pH 7.32, lactate 2.4 mmol/L (<2)

lead_in: What is the most likely diagnosis and immediate management?

options.text: Persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn; commence inhaled nitric oxide 20 ppm, intubate for high-frequency ventilation and start dopamine 5 microgram/kg/min inotropic support
Total anomalous pulmonary venous return; commence PGE1 infusion at 10 nanogram/kg/min IV, intubate and refer for urgent surgical repair as PGE1 alone will not stabilise this lesion sufficiently
Tetralogy of Fallot with hypercyanotic spell; give morphine 0.1 mg/kg IM, knee-to-chest positioning, IV fluid bolus and beta-blockade to increase systemic vascular resistance and improve saturations
Transposition of the great arteries; commence PGE1 infusion at 10 nanogram/kg/min IV, intubate for retrieval and arrange urgent NETS transfer to a cardiac centre for balloon atrial septostomy
Critical aortic coarctation; commence PGE1 infusion at 10 nanogram/kg/min IV, intubate for retrieval and arrange urgent NETS transfer for surgical repair via subclavian flap or end-to-end anastomosis

stem: You are the paediatric registrar admitting a 3-year-old boy after five days of unremitting fever to 39.6 degrees Celsius. His mother reports he has been miserable, not eating, and his eyes have become red without any discharge. On examination you find a diffuse maculopapular rash across the trunk, an erythematous strawberry tongue with cracked lips, and a single tender left cervical lymph node measuring 1.8 cm. His hands and feet are firm and swollen with a dusky red hue over the palms and soles. There is no pus behind the tonsils. His BCG scar is inflamed. Urinalysis shows sterile pyuria.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 148, blood pressure 96/58, respiratory rate 30, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 39.4 degrees Celsius
data_table.Investigations: white cells 18.2 x10^9/L (5.0-15.0), platelets 542 x10^9/L (150-400), CRP 148 mg/L (<5), ESR 78 mm/h (<15), sodium 132 mmol/L (135-145), albumin 28 g/L (35-50), ALT 78 U/L (<40)
data_table.Examination: Bilateral non-purulent bulbar conjunctival injection with limbic sparing, brawny oedema of dorsum of hands and feet, injected pharynx without exudate

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Admit for intravenous immunoglobulin 2 g/kg single infusion plus anti-inflammatory-dose aspirin now
Admit for intravenous flucloxacillin plus paired blood cultures for suspected scalded skin syndrome
Prescribe oral cefalexin 33 mg/kg every 8 hours for scarlet fever and general practice review in 48 hours
Give a single dose of intramuscular ceftriaxone plus oral amoxicillin for likely bacterial cervical adenitis
Reassure the family this is a viral exanthem and discharge with oral fluid and paracetamol advice

stem: You are the paediatric registrar admitting a 4-month-old infant with a 2-day history of coryza and worsening cough. He was born at term and is otherwise well. Feeding has dropped to 40% of usual over the last 12 hours. Wet nappies remain regular. On admission at 22:00 you commenced nasal prong oxygen at 1 litre per minute for SpO2 of 87% and moderate work of breathing. It is now 00:15. The nurse reports his SpO2 has settled at 90%, respiratory rate has come down from 68 to 56, and he took 60 mL of formula 45 minutes ago without vomiting. Chest examination reveals widespread wheeze and fine crackles bilaterally with mild subcostal recession.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 148, respiratory rate 56, SpO2 90% on nasal prong 1 L/min, temperature 37.9 degrees Celsius
data_table.Work of breathing: Mild subcostal recession, no head bob, no grunt, alert and consolable
data_table.Feeding: 60 mL of 90 mL feed taken 45 minutes ago, no vomiting, 3 wet nappies in last 12 hours

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Escalate to high-flow nasal cannula humidified oxygen at 2 L/kg/min inspired flow now
Continue nasal prong oxygen at 1 L/min and reassess response 1 hour after commencing oxygen
Trial nebulised salbutamol 2.5 mg with reassessment of work of breathing 20 minutes later
Switch to nasogastric feeds at 100 mL/kg/day and cease all oral feeding for 24 hours
Wean nasal prong oxygen off completely and check room-air saturations 10 minutes later

stem: You are the paediatric intern reviewing a 3-hour-old term male on the postnatal ward. His mother has diet-controlled gestational diabetes and he weighed 4310 g at birth (95th centile). He has fed well twice on the breast since delivery. The midwife checked a pre-feed blood sugar because of his birthweight. He is pink, alert and rooting for a feed. Temperature is stable, tone is normal, and there is no jitteriness or respiratory distress. There are no other risk factors. The bedside meter reads 1.9 mmol/L; a paired laboratory sample has been sent.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 138, respiratory rate 42, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 36.8 degrees Celsius, capillary refill 2 seconds
data_table.Feeding: Two effective breastfeeds since birth, latching well, no vomits, no jitters
data_table.Investigations: Bedside blood glucose 1.9 mmol/L (>=2.6), paired plasma glucose pending

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Reassure the mother the reading is expected in the first 24 hours and simply repeat the pre-feed check
Give an intravenous bolus of 10% dextrose 2.5 mL/kg and admit the infant to the special care nursery
Give 40% dextrose buccal gel 200 mg/kg with an immediate breastfeed and recheck 30 minutes after feeding
Commence donor expressed breast milk 20 mL/kg/day by nasogastric tube and skip the maternal breastfeed
Wait for the paired laboratory plasma glucose result before acting because bedside meters are inaccurate

stem: You are the paediatric registrar in an emergency department. A 14-year-old girl (weight 42 kg) presents 15 minutes after eating a peanut-contaminated dessert at a birthday party. She has known peanut allergy and hypertrophic cardiomyopathy for which she takes atenolol 25 mg daily. Her mother administered her EpiPen 300 mcg intramuscularly 3 minutes ago on the way in. On arrival she has stridor, generalised urticaria and is agitated. Blood pressure is 78/44, pulse 96 with poor volume, respiratory rate 32, SpO2 92% on room air, wheeze and mild subcostal recession, and hoarse voice. She is not yet cyanotic and remains alert. A second IM adrenaline dose has just been given.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 96, blood pressure 78/44, respiratory rate 32, SpO2 92% on 15 L non-rebreather, temperature 36.7 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Generalised urticaria, mild angioedema of lips, stridor with hoarse voice, wheeze with mild recession, cool peripheries, no cyanosis, alert and following commands
data_table.Medications: Atenolol 25 mg daily for HCM, EpiPen 300 mcg IM given by mother at scene, further 300 mcg IM given at arrival

lead_in: Despite two IM adrenaline doses she remains hypotensive and stridorous. What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Administer intravenous hydrocortisone 100 mg over 5 minutes as second-line therapy for refractory anaphylaxis
Administer intravenous chlorphenamine 10 mg over 5 minutes as second-line therapy for refractory anaphylaxis
Start intravenous adrenaline infusion plus a 20 mL/kg saline bolus, and prepare glucagon for beta-blocker refractoriness
Administer nebulised salbutamol 5 mg on high-flow oxygen and defer any further intramuscular adrenaline dosing
Perform emergency needle cricothyroidotomy given the stridor and hoarse voice suggesting laryngeal obstruction

stem: You are the paediatric consultant in a community adolescent mental health clinic. A 15-year-old girl has moderate-to-severe major depressive disorder confirmed on structured assessment. Symptoms have persisted 5 months. She has completed 12 sessions of CBT with a skilled psychologist without meaningful change in her PHQ-A score (still 17). She has anhedonia, hopelessness, weight loss, and passive suicidal thoughts without plan. She has no bipolar family history, no manic features, no psychotic symptoms, and no substance use. She has never taken psychotropic medication. Baseline ECG shows sinus rhythm with QTc 410 ms and normal FBC, UEC, TFTs. She and her mother are willing to consider medication with regular clinic review.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 68, blood pressure 108/64, respiratory rate 14, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.6 degrees Celsius
data_table.Investigations: PHQ-A 17 (moderate-severe), TSH 2.4 mIU/L (0.4-4.0), full blood count within normal limits, electrolytes within normal limits, ECG sinus rhythm QTc 410 ms
data_table.History: 12 sessions of CBT with psychologist without change, anhedonia, weight loss, passive suicidal ideation without plan, no bipolar history, no substances, no medication

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate first-line pharmacotherapy?

options.text: Citalopram 10 mg once daily titrated to 20 mg once daily over 2 weeks with weekly monitoring for adverse effects
Sertraline 25 mg once daily titrated to 50 mg once daily over 2 weeks with weekly monitoring for adverse effects
Venlafaxine XR 37.5 mg once daily titrated to 75 mg once daily over 2 weeks with weekly monitoring
Fluoxetine 10 mg once daily titrated to 20 mg once daily over 1 to 2 weeks with weekly monitoring for adverse effects
Mirtazapine 15 mg nightly titrated to 30 mg nightly over 2 weeks with weekly monitoring for adverse effects

stem: You are the paediatric registrar assessing a 5-month-old infant brought to the emergency department by his mother, who says he rolled off the bed 30 minutes ago. He is now crying but consolable. On examination there is bruising over the right cheek and behind the left ear, a small oval bruise on the anterior chest wall, and swelling of the right thigh with reluctance to bear weight on that leg. A brief screen shows he cannot yet roll from prone to supine or supine to prone. The mother appears anxious and the father sits quietly separated from the family. Radiograph of the right femur shows a mid-shaft spiral fracture. There is no prior child protection concern documented in the state health record.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 132, blood pressure 92/58, respiratory rate 32, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.9 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Bruises over right cheek, behind left ear, anterior chest oval bruise; right thigh swelling with reluctance to bear weight, moves other limbs symmetrically; anterior fontanelle soft and flat; developmentally cannot yet roll
data_table.Investigations: Right femur radiograph shows mid-shaft spiral fracture, full blood count within normal limits, coagulation profile within normal limits, LFTs normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial management step?

options.text: Reassure the family and apply a temporary femoral splint with orthopaedic fracture-clinic review at 24 hours
Test for osteogenesis imperfecta and copper deficiency before considering any child protection notification
Send the infant home with mother once the femoral splint is applied and give safety-net telephone advice only
Ask the mother to leave the room and ask the father directly whether he shook or dropped the child in question
Admit for evaluation, notify state child protection today, and arrange skeletal survey plus CT head plus eye review

subtopic_detail: Neonatal seizure with normal blood glucose
stem: You are the neonatal registrar called to a term-born day 2 male infant on the postnatal ward. Birthweight 3410 g, Apgar 9 and 9 at 1 and 5 minutes, uncomplicated pregnancy and delivery, mother well and afebrile, no perinatal risk factors identified, breastfeeding established. The nurse describes a 90-second episode of tonic-clonic movement of the left arm with lip smacking, apnoea to SpO2 of 82%, and eye deviation to the left. Postictally he is drowsy but rousable. Bedside blood glucose is 3.4 mmol/L, capillary blood gas is normal, temperature is 36.9 degrees Celsius, no history of maternal opioid or SSRI exposure. His father reports that his own brother had recurrent neonatal seizures that resolved by 6 months without long-term epilepsy.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 148, respiratory rate 42, SpO2 98% on room air post-event, temperature 36.9 degrees Celsius, capillary refill 2 seconds
data_table.Examination: Anterior fontanelle soft flat, tone normal, moro symmetric, no dysmorphic features, no skin lesions on Wood's lamp, cord well healed, no organomegaly, no bruises
data_table.Investigations: Bedside glucose 3.4 mmol/L (>2.6), capillary blood gas within normal limits, full blood count within normal limits, C-reactive protein 3 mg/L (<5), calcium ionised 1.20 mmol/L (1.10-1.30), magnesium 0.82 mmol/L (0.70-1.10), sodium 138 mmol/L (135-145)
data_table.History: Term uncomplicated pregnancy, no maternal opioid or SSRI exposure, family history of paternal uncle with self-resolving neonatal seizures

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Commence oral phenytoin 5 mg/kg every 12 hours and discharge to the postnatal ward on standard observations
Reassure the family this is likely jitteriness given the normal blood glucose and observe on the postnatal ward
Give intramuscular vitamin K 1 mg and observe on the postnatal ward for further seizure activity before any workup
Transfer to special care nursery for septic screen, empirical antibiotics plus aciclovir, EEG, MRI and metabolic panel
Perform a diagnostic lumbar puncture only and manage empirically as bacterial meningitis given the family history

subtopic_detail: Newly diagnosed ITP with wet purpura
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar reviewing a previously well 4-year-old boy brought by his mother because he woke this morning with numerous small purple spots on his legs and trunk, and this afternoon developed a nosebleed that lasted 20 minutes needing pressure. Two weeks ago he had a viral upper respiratory tract infection which has resolved. He looks systemically well, active, and afebrile.

Examination reveals scattered petechiae over the trunk and limbs, three small ecchymoses on the shins, blood in the nares and dry blood at the lips, mild bleeding gums when he yawns. Abdomen is soft with no organomegaly, no lymphadenopathy, no bone tenderness.

Full blood count: haemoglobin 118 g/L (110-140), white cell count 8.2 x10^9/L (4-12), neutrophils 3.6 x10^9/L, lymphocytes 4.0 x10^9/L, platelets 6 x10^9/L (150-400). Film shows large platelets, no blasts. Coagulation profile normal.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 108, blood pressure 100/62, respiratory rate 22, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.8 degrees Celsius
data_table.Bloods: Hb 118 g/L (110-140), WCC 8.2 x10^9/L (4-12), platelets 6 x10^9/L (150-400), film large platelets no blasts, coags normal
data_table.Exam: petechiae, bruises, active epistaxis, bleeding gums, no organomegaly, no lymphadenopathy

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Discharge home with observation only, arrange platelet count in 48 hours, avoid contact sports and NSAIDs
Admit and administer intravenous immunoglobulin 0.8 g/kg as a single dose with paracetamol pre-medication
Transfuse a single unit of pooled platelets to raise the count acutely and prevent further mucosal bleeding
Perform bone marrow aspirate today to exclude leukaemia before commencing any specific therapy for this presentation
Commence prednisolone 4 mg/kg daily for 4 days without further investigation and review platelet count at day 7

stem:
You are the paediatric registrar reviewing an 8-year-old girl 6 hours into treatment of new type 1 diabetes with severe diabetic ketoacidosis. On admission her pH was 7.02, bicarbonate 6 mmol/L, glucose 32 mmol/L, ketones 5.8 mmol/L. She received a 10 mL/kg 0.9 percent saline bolus and has been on 0.9 percent saline with potassium at maintenance plus 5 percent deficit replacement over 48 hours, with an insulin infusion at 0.05 unit/kg/hour. Her glucose has fallen from 32 to 14 mmol/L. She had been chatty and reading her book.

At this review she complains of a new headache, has vomited once, and is now more drowsy (GCS 12: E3V4M5). Blood pressure has risen from 108/64 to 138/86 and her pulse has fallen from 118 to 68. There is no papilloedema visible but pupils are equal and reactive. Her most recent electrolytes show sodium 138, glucose 12, and pH 7.22.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 68 (was 118), blood pressure 138/86 (was 108/64), respiratory rate 18, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.8 degrees Celsius
data_table.Progress: 6 hours DKA Rx, glucose 32 to 12, pH 7.02 to 7.22
data_table.Neuro: new headache, one vomit, GCS 12 (E3V4M5), pupils equal and reactive

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate intervention?

options.text: Increase the insulin infusion to 0.1 unit/kg/hour and add dextrose 10 percent to accelerate resolution of acidosis and ketogenesis
Administer another 20 mL/kg 0.9 percent saline bolus to correct hypovolaemia given her drowsiness and headache
Give 3 percent saline 3 mL/kg over 15 minutes or mannitol 0.5 g/kg, reduce fluid rate by one-third, arrange CT after treatment
Arrange an immediate CT head to confirm cerebral oedema before commencing any specific therapy for the neurological deterioration
Give sodium bicarbonate 1 mmol/kg IV to correct the residual metabolic acidosis and improve cerebral perfusion during recovery

stem:
You are the paediatric registrar reviewing a 9-month-old boy who has had a temperature of 39 to 40 degrees Celsius for 6 days. He has been listless, refused feeds intermittently, and had a single loose stool this morning. On examination today: irritable but consolable, a diffuse maculopapular rash across the trunk that has been present 3 days, mild bilateral non-purulent conjunctival injection, dry cracked lips without oral ulcers, no lymphadenopathy, no peripheral changes. He has not had a coryzal illness. No known unwell contacts.

Bloods: haemoglobin 96 g/L (105-135), white cell count 18.2 x10^9/L (5-15), neutrophils 12.6 x10^9/L, platelets 512 x10^9/L (150-450), CRP 118 mg/L (below 5), ESR 82 mm/h, albumin 24 g/L (35-50), ALT 88 U/L (below 40), sodium 132 mmol/L. Urinalysis shows sterile pyuria. Blood cultures at 24 h are negative. Chest X-ray is clear.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 148, blood pressure 92/58, respiratory rate 32, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 39.4 degrees Celsius
data_table.Bloods: Hb 96 g/L, WCC 18.2 x10^9/L, platelets 512 x10^9/L, CRP 118 mg/L (<5), ESR 82 mm/h, albumin 24 g/L (35-50), ALT 88 U/L (<40)
data_table.Urine: sterile pyuria on dipstick and microscopy

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Start high-dose oral prednisolone 2 mg/kg daily for 5 days for a suspected autoimmune inflammatory process while awaiting further tests
Continue empirical IV ceftriaxone 50 mg/kg daily and repeat sepsis workup at 48 hours if fever persists before considering IVIG
Discharge home with paracetamol pending viral swab result and community follow-up in 3 to 5 days to reassess response
Arrange echocardiography now, treat as incomplete Kawasaki disease with IVIG 2 g/kg over 10 to 12 hours and aspirin 3 to 5 mg/kg/day
Add IV vancomycin and admit for observation; hold immunoglobulin until infection is definitely excluded on microbiology

stem:
You are the neonatal registrar reviewing a 60-hour-old term baby born at 39+2 weeks by normal vaginal delivery, birth weight 3.4 kg. Mother has blood group O positive with anti-A antibodies. Baby was noted to be visibly jaundiced by 24 hours of age. He has been feeding briefly but not vigorously, passing 3 wet nappies over the past 12 hours, and lost 6 percent of birth weight.

Baby is now lethargic with a poor cry and reduced tone. Cephalocaudal jaundice extends to soles of feet. He is afebrile, saturating well in air, no bruising, no cephalohaematoma. There is no organomegaly. Bilirubin at admission was 340 micromol/L, now at 60 hours it is 512 micromol/L. Direct antiglobulin test is positive. Baby's blood group is A positive. Reticulocyte count is 8 percent (0.5 to 2). Haemoglobin 128 g/L (145 to 225 at 24 hours). He is on triple-bank intensive phototherapy for the past 4 hours.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 158, blood pressure 62/38, respiratory rate 44, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.5 degrees Celsius
data_table.Bloods: total bilirubin 512 umol/L (age 60h phototherapy line ~380, exchange line ~430), DAT positive, retic 8%, Hb 128 g/L, ABO incompatibility
data_table.Rx so far: triple bank intensive phototherapy 4 hours, IV fluids commenced

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Continue intensive phototherapy alone and repeat serum bilirubin in 6 hours before deciding on exchange transfusion
Stop phototherapy to prevent riboflavin depletion and give oral ursodeoxycholic acid 20 mg/kg/day until bilirubin falls
Give a top-up transfusion of packed red cells 10 mL/kg to correct the anaemia, then observe with phototherapy for 12 hours
Administer intravenous phenobarbital 15 mg/kg loading dose to induce hepatic conjugation of unconjugated bilirubin
Prepare for double-volume exchange transfusion urgently while continuing intensive phototherapy and giving IVIG 0.5 g/kg for immune haemolysis

stem:
You are the paediatric registrar reviewing an 8-year-old girl who presented three weeks ago with palpable purpura over her buttocks and lower limbs, symmetrical ankle and knee joint swelling, and colicky abdominal pain. She was diagnosed with IgA vasculitis (previously called Henoch-Schonlein purpura). Her purpura and abdominal pain resolved with paracetamol; joint swelling settled.

Weekly urinalysis for surveillance now shows blood 3+ and protein 3+. Her spot urine protein/creatinine ratio is 320 mg/mmol (below 20). Serum albumin is 24 g/L (35 to 50), creatinine 78 umol/L (30 to 60 for her age), estimated GFR 62 mL/min/1.73 m2. Her blood pressure is 132/86 which is above the 95th centile for age, sex, and height. She has periorbital and pretibial oedema. Complement C3 and C4 are normal.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 96, blood pressure 132/86 (>95th centile), respiratory rate 20, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.6 degrees Celsius
data_table.Bloods: creatinine 78 umol/L (30-60), eGFR 62 mL/min/1.73 m2, albumin 24 g/L (35-50), C3 normal, C4 normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Refer to paediatric nephrology urgently and arrange renal biopsy plus commence oral prednisolone pending histology and steroid-based induction
Continue weekly urine surveillance for another 6 months and reassess if proteinuria persists or worsens further
Start oral amoxicillin 25 mg/kg 8-hourly empirically for possible post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis pending ASOT results
Restrict dietary salt and fluid and reassess urinalysis and blood pressure in 4 weeks at the local General practice for review
Commence enalapril 0.1 mg/kg daily for the hypertension and continue outpatient monitoring monthly without further investigation

stem:
You are the paediatric registrar called to ED for a 3-year-old boy with 4 days of fever, sore throat, and increasing neck stiffness. Today he has developed drooling, refuses to swallow, and holds his neck extended. He is anxious, sits upright on his father's lap, muffled voice, mild stridor at rest, no drooling on arrival. Temperature 39.4, pulse 148, respiratory rate 34, SpO2 96 percent on room air.

He will not open his mouth for examination. There is a visible swelling in the posterior pharyngeal wall on limited view. There is tender cervical lymphadenopathy.
